hypothesis: The ETF panel is fit for systematic research after validation and an explicit missing-data policy, with no observation deleted.
notes: Zero blocking errors. All 20%+ moves corroborated by peer returns and volume, so retained. Known residual bias: the universe consists of ETFs that survive today (§7.5.2).

hypothesis: A 15-ETF multi-asset universe contains far fewer independent risk dimensions than it contains assets, and that number falls further in crises.
notes: PC1 (equity vs duration) and PC2 (rates level) dominate. Only a handful of eigenvalues clear the Marchenko-Pastur noise bound, so covariance shrinkage is justified before optimisation rather than after it disappoints.

hypothesis: Daily ETF returns are not normally distributed, so parametric VaR will understate the tail.
notes: Every asset rejects normality at any conventional level. Historical simulation is the default VaR method in Stage 9 as a direct result.

hypothesis: Does GARCH(1,1) materially improve volatility forecasts over simpler rolling and EWMA estimators? (spec §32)
notes: GARCH wins on QLIKE but a short-half-life EWMA wins on correlation and R^2 at a fraction of the complexity. EWMA is kept as the production estimator; GARCH is retained as a documented extension, not adopted.

hypothesis: vol scaled 126 momentum predicts subsequent 21-day cross-sectional ETF returns.
notes: IC +0.0122, p=0.7753: no evidence of predictive content. At the family level, 15 of 72 tests clear a naive 5% threshold against 3.6 expected by chance, and 10 survive Benjamini-Hochberg control with the hypothesised positive sign. Cross-sectional momentum across heterogeneous asset classes is a much weaker effect than the within-equity version the literature usually reports: the cross-section here is dominated by the volatility difference between bonds and commodities rather than by relative trend. The signal is carried forward to the backtest anyway, so that the portfolio-level result can be compared against this signal-level evidence rather than replacing it.
train_period: 2006-04-10 to 2015-12-31 (development sample)

hypothesis: The 21-day price z-score is NEGATIVELY related to subsequent 5-day returns (mean-reversion hypothesis, beta < 0).
notes: IC +0.0089, p=0.6496: no evidence of predictive content. At the family level, 6 of 72 tests clear a naive 5% threshold against 3.6 expected by chance, and 5 survive Benjamini-Hochberg control with the hypothesised negative sign: zscore_ranked_5@h1, zscore_5@h1, zscore_10@h1, zscore_ranked_10@h1, reversal_5@h1. Every survivor sits at the 1-day horizon with a short lookback, so the effect is real but decays almost immediately. That decay profile, not the peak IC, sets the tradable holding period, and a 1-day holding period means transaction costs will decide whether any of it survives -- which Stage 6 tests directly.
train_period: 2006-04-10 to 2015-12-31 (development sample)

hypothesis: Correcting for overlapping observations materially changes the evidence for both signal families, and the Fundamental Law implies only a modest information ratio even before costs.
notes: Naive standard errors understate uncertainty by up to 3.3x on overlapping forward returns. Both families' information is concentrated at 1-5 days, where the implied pre-cost information ratio is at its highest and the required turnover is also at its highest -- the central tension the backtest must resolve. Momentum and reversion signals are close to uncorrelated in the cross-section, which is the precondition for the strategy-level diversification tested in Stage 10.

hypothesis: M3_momentum generates positive risk-adjusted returns after realistic transaction costs.
notes: Turnover of 9.2x per year costs 57 bps annually at the 10 bps baseline, taking the Sharpe ratio from 0.38 gross to 0.30 net. The strategy breaks even at 27.8 bps. This is the direct consequence of Stage 5's finding that the predictive information sits at the 1-5 day horizon: the only way to harvest it is to trade constantly, and the trading costs more than the signal is worth.

hypothesis: Sophisticated portfolio optimisation improves risk-adjusted returns over naive equal weighting.
notes: The best model on full-sample net Sharpe is M1_inverse_vol. The risk-based allocators, which use no expected returns at all, beat every book that requires estimating mu. The estimation-error experiment explains why: an unconstrained optimiser holds 3 of 15 assets with a 77% maximum weight, and a perturbation of mu worth 25% of its cross-sectional dispersion moves up to 92% of the book. This is a full-sample comparison and therefore in-sample; Stage 11 re-runs it walk-forward before any conclusion is drawn.

hypothesis: Which covariance and volatility estimators produce the most useful out-of-sample risk forecasts? (spec §33)
notes: EWMA forecasts risk most accurately; shrinkage's contribution is conditioning, cutting the condition number from 35609 to 9764. Those are different goods and the distinction matters: an optimiser inverts the covariance matrix, so it is hurt far more by an ill-conditioned matrix than by a slightly less accurate one. The production configuration therefore uses EWMA for position sizing and shrinkage for anything that gets inverted. GARCH(1,1) is retained as a documented extension only: its mean persistence of 0.993 implies volatility shocks that decay over months, and it is integrated for 2 of 15 assets.

hypothesis: The VaR model is validated out of sample: breaches arrive at the promised rate and are independent through time.
notes: Rejected, and this is the most useful negative result in the project. Every method fails at 99% -- historical simulation breaches 1.48% of days against 1% promised -- and every method fails the Christoffersen independence test at 95%: the breach count is roughly right but the breaches arrive in clusters, because an unconditional model cannot represent volatility clustering. The practical consequence is that a single VaR number is not a risk limit; it must be paired with CVaR (whose realised/predicted ratio is 1.03, well calibrated) and with the regime analysis.

hypothesis: Risk-based allocation survives the post-COVID inflation shock better than equity beta does (Ch. 19 closing case study).
notes: 2022 is the regime that breaks the equity/bond diversification these books rely on: both legs fell together, so risk-based allocation had nowhere to hide. The regime correlation table quantifies it directly.

hypothesis: Combining strategy return streams improves risk-adjusted performance beyond the best individual strategy (Ch. 22 §22.5).
notes: The return streams are weakly correlated on average (+0.24), so combining does raise the Sharpe ratio above the *average* component. Whether it beats the *best* component is the sterner test and the one reported here: 0.78 versus 0.87. Combination is not alchemy -- it cannot turn two strategies with no edge into one that has an edge, and Stage 6 established that the alpha strategies have no edge net of costs. What it does is reduce the variance of the total, which is worth having when the components are genuinely positive.

hypothesis: The backtest engine and every production strategy are free of look-ahead bias.
notes: Perturbing all post-split data leaves every pre-split weight bit-identical for the production strategies, while the deliberately broken control strategy (built from tomorrow's return) is caught at every split date and in both perturbation modes. A test that never fails proves nothing, which is why the control is part of the suite rather than a one-off check.

hypothesis: momentum performance is robust across its parameter family, not the product of one fortunate choice.
notes: 75% of the 24 parameter combinations produce a positive net Sharpe ratio, with a best of 0.30 against a median of 0.08. Verdict: plateau: results are broadly similar across parameters

hypothesis: Out-of-sample walk-forward performance justifies the model ladder's added complexity.
notes: The best out-of-sample model is M1_inverse_vol at a Sharpe ratio of 0.84, with a block-bootstrap 90% interval of [0.41, 1.28]. The interval is what the headline number should be read against: a Sharpe ratio of 0.8 over twenty years still carries an interval wide enough to contain materially worse outcomes, and nothing in this project is precise enough to distinguish the top few models from one another.

hypothesis: Final model comparison: which step of the ladder actually improved risk-adjusted returns after costs? (spec §55-§56)
notes: M1_inverse_vol has the highest full-sample net Sharpe ratio at 0.87, against 0.70 for equal weight and 0.65 for SPY buy-and-hold. The improvement over the naive benchmark comes almost entirely from risk-based weighting, not from alpha: every model that requires estimating expected returns lands below the models that do not.

hypothesis: Cointegrated pairs within this ETF universe produce tradable relative-value returns after costs (Extension E, Ch. 22 §22.3.3-4).
notes: Pairs were selected by cointegration on the development sample only and then traded over the whole history with that hedge ratio, so the later portion is genuinely out of sample. The screen is the discipline: a pair that is 0.95 correlated but not cointegrated has a spread that can wander off forever, and trading it is a bet on nothing.

hypothesis: Nonlinear machine learning provides genuine out-of-sample economic improvement over the simpler econometric and systematic models (spec §47).
notes: The model with the best AUC (ML2_random_forest) is also the model with the best net Sharpe ratio (ML2_random_forest), which is the point of evaluating on three axes: classification accuracy weights a 0.1% day and a 5% day equally, and trading does not. All four models trade at high turnover for a small edge and land in the same place as the classical signals in Stage 6. ML is not rejected because it is ML; it is rejected because the underlying predictability at this horizon is too small to pay for the turnover required to harvest it, and no functional form changes that.

hypothesis: HRP and HERC produce more stable weights than minimum-variance optimisation under estimation noise (Lopez de Prado's central claim).
notes: Decision rule fixed in advance on weight dispersion: retain if the hierarchical methods are more stable than minimum variance in at least 75% of windows, reject if in at most 25%. The verdict follows that rule. It does NOT mean minimum variance is better behaved: it holds 3.6 assets with a 97% maximum weight, so its weights cannot move -- the Stage 7 lesson that a book can be 'stable' by sitting in a corner. The risk-inflation columns are POST-HOC (added after seeing the dispersion result) and are reported as a diagnostic, not as grounds to overturn the declared decision.

hypothesis: HRP / HERC deliver a statistically better net Sharpe ratio than risk parity out of sample.
notes: Judged by the paired bootstrap with Benjamini-Hochberg control across all 15 model pairs. 'Better' requires a significant difference in the right direction; a higher point estimate is not enough.

hypothesis: Macro features improve out-of-sample forecasts of monthly asset-class excess returns beyond what price features already provide.
notes: Rule fixed in advance: retain if at least one sleeve passes Clark-West at FDR 10% for price+macro vs price AND the mean OOS R-squared of that comparison is positive. Only 177 monthly out-of-sample observations per sleeve, and the 13 macro features carry about 5.3 independent dimensions, so there is little independent information to find and little power to find it. A null here is weak evidence of absence, not strong evidence of it. Nested comparisons use Clark-West because a plain Diebold-Mariano test is mechanically undersized on nested models. The test sample starts in 2011 because the standardised features, 60 training months and 12-month momentum all have to exist first.
train_period: expanding window from the start of data

hypothesis: Ignoring publication lags inflates the apparent out-of-sample skill of macro features.
notes: A methodology control, not an alpha hypothesis. This entry was first drafted with the literal rule 'retain if R-squared inflation > 0'; the measured inflation of +0.04 percentage points of R-squared on the pre-declared comparison shows that rule could not tell an effect from noise, and the control was never meant to gate a decision, so it is recorded rather than retained or rejected (the original wording is in the git history). The post-hoc numbers ask the question that matters for the decision: on price+macro vs price the inflation is +0.48 percentage points, and the direct Diebold-Mariano tests of whether ignoring lags makes the same model forecast better find 0 of 10 sleeve-model pairs significant after BH control. Reading: ignoring publication lags flatters the numbers a little but does not manufacture significance here, because the lags are two to six weeks and the features barely forecast monthly returns even with the extra look; there is little to inflate. The availability machinery is kept because it is correct by construction, not because this sample demanded it.

hypothesis: A signal built from price and macro, f(price, macro), beats the price-only signal after transaction costs.

hypothesis: DCC-GARCH covariance forecasts have a lower out-of-sample loss than each of the sample, EWMA and shrinkage estimators.
notes: Retained only if the mean loss is lower than each static estimator's AND all three tests are significant after BH control. The mean loss is lowest for DCC against all three, but the differences are driven by a few stress months and are not significant at this sample size. Post-hoc: DCC has the lower loss on only 41% of origins against the sample estimator and 33% against EWMA, but 64% against shrinkage: in a typical month the static estimators are as good or better, in a crisis they are far worse, and a mean-based test sees mostly the second. One origin, 2020-02-28, accounts for 89% of the total difference against the sample estimator (post-hoc).

hypothesis: A filtered high-volatility HMM state at the close of day t predicts larger absolute equity-sleeve returns on day t+1.
notes: The easy case: volatility clusters, so a state defined by volatility should forecast it, and a model that could not would be broken. Retained as a sanity check, not as a trading result. With daily data the model's two states are short volatility clusters, not bull and bear markets: the full-sample fit implies a mean spell of 7 days in the high-volatility state and 20 in the calm one. Decision rules were committed to config/regimes.yaml (commit 43522cb) before any regime result existed. One methodological change was made after the first look at the results: the circular-shift statistic was studentised. The plain difference of means had put three rare, high-variance flags (3-state high-vol, top-quintile volatility, bear market) across the line; a size simulation then showed the plain statistic rejecting a TRUE null 36% of the time for a rare high-variance regime against 3% for the studentised one. Decisions follow the studentised statistic; both p-values are in stage16_permutation_tests.csv.
train_period: expanding window from the start of data, refit every 126 days after the first 750

hypothesis: Bayesian online change-point detection flags dated volatility shocks within 60 trading days with few false alarms.
notes: By the pre-declared rule an alarm episode must START on or after the dated event. Three events were missed only in that sense: the detector fired one to four trading days BEFORE the date, on the same sell-offs, and those episodes are scored as false alarms. Crediting alarms up to 5 days early (post-hoc, labelled, not used for the decision) gives 5/5 detected at 0.86 false alarms a year. Most 'false alarms' are real market stress that simply is not on the list of five. The one-line volatility-jump rule detects all five at its pre-declared setting with longer delays and more alarms, and at a stricter post-hoc setting matches BOCPD's false-alarm rate with a shorter delay: the Bayesian machinery is not shown to beat it on these events.

hypothesis: De-risking an equal-weight book toward cash as the filtered HMM high-volatility probability rises beats equal weight after costs.
notes: Judged by the pre-declared family (RA1 vs equal weight; RA2 vs equal weight and vs risk parity; RA3 vs momentum), paired stationary bootstrap, Benjamini-Hochberg across the four comparisons; a strategy is retained only if every comparison it appears in is significant with a POSITIVE difference. A higher point estimate without significance is not an improvement. The same overlay driven by a one-line rule (expanding volatility percentile above the 80th) reaches a net Sharpe of 0.928 against the HMM's 0.915, with a maximum drawdown of -13.7% against -17.2%: a slower state estimate suits a monthly overlay better than the HMM's one-to-three-week clusters.

hypothesis: A backtest on smoothed (full-sample) HMM probabilities overstates the honest, filtered one, and the automated look-ahead test tells them apart.
notes: Two questions with different answers. (1) Does the automated test work? Every honest rule passed (16/16) and every look-ahead control (smoothed, or filtered with full-sample parameters) was flagged (20/20), with pre-split weights that moved when only the future was replaced. (2) Does hindsight inflate the Sharpe ratio? At the monthly overlay it did not here (honest 0.915, smoothed 0.900): regimes last one to three weeks, a monthly overlay samples one day in twenty, and the smoothed probabilities see only a few days past it. At a weekly overlay (post-hoc) honest 0.879, smoothed 0.914 (difference +0.035, p=0.42). A leak need not show up in the headline number to be a leak; that is why the test exists.
